newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Internet rules could close rich-poor gap-US advise.
newsitem.headline: Internet rules could close rich-poor gap-US advise.

text.p: The gap between rich and poor nations could widen if developing countries do not join a U.S. initiative to create a global framework for Internet trade, a senior White House adviser said on Monday.
"For countries that are poor and stay away from it, it could widen the gap," Ira Magaziner, senior adviser for policy development to President Bill Clinton, told a news conference.
"I think they would be cheating their citizens out of their economic future," he said.

Magaziner was in Singapore to brief government and business officials on the nine-point Framework for Global Electronic Commerce before leaving to address an Internet conference in Malaysia scheduled for Tuesday.
The document covers issues of taxation and tariffs, a uniform commercial code, electronic payments, technical standards, contracts, privacy, content, inter-operability and encryption.
He pointed to Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea and nations in the European Union as key Internet users, and said getting a critical mass to back the framework was important.
But he said the framework was not intended to create a U.S.-approved set of access, content and legal standards.
"We're not trying to impose our values or our definitions of what is illegal on another country," Magaziner said.
He said the framework would help market forces establish the rules by which people wanted the Internet run.
Governments should be hands-off when regulating electronic commerce or face the prospect of spending the next 30 years undoing bad regulation that could stifle Internet trade, he added.
Magaziner predicted Internet trade could account for as much as 20 percent of global retail sales or tens of billions of dollars within a decade.
It would double every year for the foreseeable future and become the "fundamental driving force bringing growth to all our economies for at least the next 25 years", he said.

With that sort of potential it was vital for developing nations to allow full Internet access to their citizens and to sign up to a framework setting standards for secure transactions that creates a recognised legal trading environment.

"Those that don't or try to cut themselves off from it will fall behind pretty quickly economically because I think this (the Internet) will be a fundamental tool for economic development," Magaziner said.
